s_7ezzd8nh4z.title: Emergency Department
s_7ezzd8nh4z.description:
Queensway Carleton Hospitalâ€™s new Emergency Department expansion is being built to meet the urgent realities of Ottawaâ€™s rapidly growing west end. The hospital was originally built in 1976 for a community of about 100,000 people, but it now serves more than 500,000 residents and remains the only full-service hospital in the cityâ€™s west end.

Today, the Emergency Department is operating far beyond its intended capacity. Designed for 63,000 visits a year, it now sees more than 83,000 visits annually and is trending toward 100,000, creating longer waits and greater strain on patients, families, and frontline teams.

This once-in-a-generation expansion will more than double the size of the Emergency Department, add 90 urgently needed inpatient beds, and bring critical diagnostic imaging such as CT and X-ray directly into the department. It will also include a dedicated mental health care space with private treatment rooms, controlled lighting, reduced noise, and a separate entrance to provide safer, more dignified care for patients in crisis.

The goal is simple: faster diagnosis, shorter wait times, improved patient flow, and better care when every minute matters. This is not just a construction project â€” it is a vital investment in readiness, safety, and care for families across Ottawaâ€™s west end.

no_uutrjfm27j.body:
The Satellite Imaging Unit will provide patients and clinical teams
with immediate access to essential diagnostic imaging close to the
Emergency Department, trauma services, and acute care treatment areas.
Its strategic location will help reduce the need to transport
vulnerable or critically ill patients through other parts of the
hospital, supporting a safer, faster, and more coordinated care
experience.

Equipped to support timely assessment and clinical decision-making,
the unit will allow physicians and care teams to obtain the diagnostic
information they need when every moment matters. Faster access to
imaging can help identify injuries, confirm diagnoses, guide treatment
plans, and determine whether a patient requires surgery, admission,
additional testing, or another level of specialized care. This
improved workflow will also help reduce delays, ease pressure on
central imaging services, and strengthen collaboration among emergency
physicians, nurses, technologists, specialists, and other members of
the care team.

For patients and families, the Satellite Imaging Unit will offer
greater comfort, privacy, and reassurance during what may be a
stressful or uncertain time. Keeping diagnostic services close to the
point of care minimizes unnecessary movement and allows patients to
remain connected to the clinical teams responsible for their
treatment.

Naming the Satellite Imaging Unit represents a meaningful opportunity
to invest in advanced diagnostic care and a more efficient,
patient-centred hospital environment. This prominent recognition will
honour a generous commitment to innovation, timely diagnosis, clinical
excellence, and improved health outcomes for patients across the
community.

no_isl00d89od.body:
The Rapid Assessment Centre will create a dedicated environment where
patients can be evaluated quickly, safely, and efficiently upon
arrival at the Emergency Department. Designed to support early
clinical assessment and faster decision-making, the Centre will bring
together physicians, nurses, diagnostic services, and other members of
the care team in a coordinated setting focused on identifying each
patientâ€™s needs as soon as possible.

By allowing appropriate tests, consultations, and initial treatments
to begin earlier, the Rapid Assessment Centre will help streamline the
patient journey and reduce unnecessary delays. Patients may be
assessed, monitored, treated, discharged, admitted, or transferred to
another area of the hospital based on the level of care they require.
This flexible model will support a more efficient use of emergency
resources while helping clinical teams respond to changing patient
volumes and increasingly complex care needs.

The Centre will also provide a more comfortable and organized
experience for patients and families during what is often a stressful
and uncertain time. Clearer care pathways, improved coordination, and
earlier communication will help patients better understand what is
happening and what the next steps in their treatment will be. For
hospital staff, the Centre will support collaboration, improve
workflow, and create a purpose-designed environment for delivering
timely, patient-centred emergency care.

A $5 million naming investment in the Rapid Assessment Centre
represents an exceptional opportunity to help transform the delivery
of emergency care. This prominent naming opportunity will recognize
visionary generosity and a lasting commitment to faster access,
clinical excellence, innovation, and better health outcomes for
patients and families throughout the community.

no_5f0c3r63zp.body:
When a seriously injured patient arrives at the hospital, every minute
matters. The trauma resuscitation centre is the part of the emergency
department dedicated to those moments. It is where a trained trauma
team comes together to rapidly assess, stabilize, and treat patients
with lifeâ€‘threatening injuries.

In this space, specialists work in parallelâ€”airway, breathing,
circulation, imaging, and surgery planning happen at the same time,
not in sequence. That coordinated response shortens the time to
critical diagnostics like CT scans and speeds decisions about surgery
or intensive care, which has been shown to reduce emergency department
length of stay and improve key indicators of trauma care quality.

For patients and families, the trauma resuscitation centre is where
fear begins to turn into a sense of safety. Studies show that clear
leadership, organized teamwork, and compassionate communication during
resuscitation help patients feel they are in capable hands, even in
the most vulnerable moments.

Investing in the trauma resuscitation centre means investing in the
systems, equipment, and training that give people their best chance of
survival and recovery when the unexpected happens.
